   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From Tony Catts, GUERNSEY


A late: Healthy, Happy and
Prosperous New Year's Greetings
to you and yours together with
my congratulations on the last 5
years' issues of the magazine.
There is no equal!

I have no idea when I can set up
my system (=Opus/Microdrive and/
or Disciple to come at present).
I do have 24 new microdrive
cartridges but still have not
come across a way of recovering
programs from the Opus!Is there?

             Yours,

              Tony

Brian Cavers to Tony Catts


To transfer Opus files to the +D
or Disciple you need to first
put them on tape and then load
them back. If you have two
separate systems you can do this
in one operation with some tape
recorders by selecting record
and pause and saving and loading
at the same time.If this doesn't
work then you can get an ampli-
fier to do this and Malcolm
Goodman has an excellent article
in this month's DRIVECHAT on
this very subject.

However, how does one actually
save and load files? Can it be
done automatically? Read on...

If you have TRANSEXPRESS then it
can automatically save from Opus
disc to tape but unfortunately,
Romantic Robot no longer produce
this software so if you haven't
got it then I can only suggest
you scour the classified adverts
or put a message in OUTBOARD.


The alternative is laborious but
I see no other way. You need an
extended CAT program to give you
details of the files. DATACAT in
OUTLET 18 can do this.

You then load and save them
manually. If you don't know how
to do this then refer to your
Opus manual and Spectrum manual.

Use UNITRANS+ (OUTLET 20)to load
files into the +D but OPENTYPE
(PRINT) files cannot be moved
this way. Tasword 3 files are of
this type but you need to ask
yourself how you will use them
from a +D anyway.An Opus Tasword
3 won't work.If you have Tasword
2 then use T3TO2 to convert the
files first (OUTLET 20).

This is the tragedy of the lack
of a standard system for the
Spectrum. It is theoretically
possible for some genius to
write a +D program that can read
an Opus disc and convert the
programs automatically but it is
a HUGE task requiring great
knowledge and skill with no real
financial reward!       - Brian

From:C. Grant Dixon, ROSS-ON-WYE

Dear Both,

Just a short line to air a
couple of grumbles. On OUTLET 51
there was not enough room to put
my "sys 3d". Additionally, I was
thinking of cataloguing all
OUTLETS using Dave Hood's "Disc

scales. I hope that you will

"Addenders".

           Best wishes

Brian Cavers to Grant Dixon

Sorry, Grant. I usually try to
leave room and the directory for
the Disciple Issue 51 does show
17K free. However, there appears
to be a directory fault because,
as you say, one cannot save even
the dos without the "disc full"
error.If you have two drives the
answer is to format a new disc
and copy the lot with...
        SAVE d1;"*" TO d2

You will then be able to save
the dos on the disc(I tried it).
You can copy the whole lot back
to the original disc if you want
but test it first! I will try to
make sure this bug does not
occur again by using the same
method.

Sorry about the delay in the
publication of your article.This
is because not only do we have a
lot of programs and articles
sent in which are forming a
"queue" but also that which you
sent consists of many different
files (including BASIC and
SCREEN$ I think) and needs a LOT
of work to prepare it for
OUTLET. I assure you that it is
not forgotten.
                     - Brian

From: Ken Stearn, FIFE


Dear Outlet,

I have just received 'OUTWRITE'
and,as expected, it is a quality
piece of work. I have bought
'OUTLET' from the start so am
well accustomed to this standard
of software. My compliments to
Bob Wilkinson.

I recently took a look at some
of the other SAM magazines on
offer and can assure you that
'OUTLET' still reigns supreme.
One mag. was even threatening
violence to another mag!! Who
says computer games don't breed
violence?

I'd like to have the following
piece of "Japanese Gaelic" (!)
translated into English so I
can use downloaded fonts on my
24-pin Toshiba printer (Epson-
compatible) connected to SAM's
communication interface. I have
typed out the relevant passage
from the manual...

       SELECT USER
ESC %  DEFINED CHARACTER SET

Function: Selects the character
          set you specify

Sequence    ESC %

Hex.        1B 25 n

Dec.        27 37 n

Discussion  The value of n is a
            binary number that
            identifies either a
            resident character
            set or a down-loaded
            one.

00H (0 decimal) Specifies a
                resident set

01H (1 decimal) Specifies a
                downloaded set

The printer ignores this command
if the font is not loaded.

ESC &   SPECIFY USER DEFINED
        CHARACTERS

Function:Specifies user
         designed character sets

Sequence:ESC & 00 n1 n2 [d1 d2
         d3 data...] n2-n1+1

Hex      1B 26 00 n1 n2 [d1 d2
         d3 data...] n2-n1+1

DEC      27 38 0  n1 n2 [d1 d2
         d3 data...] n2-n1+1


Discussion: All parameters are
binary numbers. n1 and n2
identify the start and end codes
to be defined.

d1 sets the amount of space you
want to add to the left of the
character, d2 the pattern width
and d3 sets the space to the
right. The parameters d1 d2 d3
must satisfy these conditions:-

            d2          d1+d2+d3
  Mode  (max.value)  (max.value)
  ----  -----------  -----------

Draft mode    9          12
LQ mode at
10 cpi       29          36

LQ mode at
12 cpi       23          30

LQ mode at
15 cpi       15          24

Proportional
pitch        38          42

The data defines the character
pattern. In normal mode, each
character requires three bytes
of data (d2*3).

A dot column represents three
data bytes in normal mode and
two data bytes in superscript/
subscript mode. The msb of the
first byte corresponds to the
top pin of the column,while the
lsb of the third byte (in normal
mode) corresponds to the bottom
pin. Each character with a code
between n1 and n2 must be
defined. This means that...

d2*3*(n2-n1+1) or d2*3*(n2-n1+1)
data bytes are required.

I have tried to load both 8-bit
and 16-bit fonts to no avail.
But of course I am at a loss as
how to enter them. I hope you
can help.
                    Ken Stearn

Brian Cavers to Ken Stearn

In BASIC, you use the LPRINT
command to send data to your
printer and each piece of data
is a number between 0 and 255.
However, the SAM Coupe and most
Spectrum printer interfaces have
two"modes" of sending this data:
as pure code or in "expanded"
form. In this expanded form many
of the codes are stopped by the
computer and instead, a keyword
is sent. This is for printing a
BASIC listing etc. To switch the
printer to do things like BOLD
printing or ITALICS you need to
send "control" codes. To do this
you need first to make sure your
computer is in the "pure code"
mode as follows...

To send control codes, first:

OPEN #3;"B"          SAM COUPE,
                     OPUS,MDRIVE

POKE @6,1            DISCIPLE/+D

FORMAT LPRINT "U"    +3

COPY: REM CHR$ 0     KEMPSTON E

After, use LPRINT to send codes.
For example, to send code 65 you
LPRINT CHR$ 65. Codes between 32
and 127 also have an "ASCII"
equivalent so you can use that
instead if you know it. To find
it just enter,e.g.,PRINT CHR$ 65
and you will see a capital A on
your computer screen so you can
use LPRINT "A" instead of the
LPRINT CHR$ 65 if you want!

I mention that because you may
wonder what the printer manual
means when it's got ESC &. This
means the code for ESC (which is
27) and "&" (code 38) so that
could be sent to the printer
with either...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;CHR$ 38;  or...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;"&";

           ...it means the same.
If you enter PRINT CHR$ 38 you
will see a "&" on your screen.If
you enter PRINT CODE "&" you
will see 38 printed on your
screen.Get it? Under the heading
ESC & in your list next to DEC
you will see it starts 27 38 0
plus other things so enter...

10 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"&";CHR$ 0;
  (tells printer,font is coming)

20 LPRINT CHR$ 32;
   (first character. - the SPACE
   character. This is n1 in your
   list)

30 LPRINT CHR$ 127;
  (last character, the copyright
  sign. This is n2 in your list)

40 LPRINT CHR$ 0;
          (left gap width before
          character. This is d1)

50 LPRINT CHR$ 16;
   (character pattern width. d2)

60 LPRINT CHR$ 4;
           (right gap width. d3)

You can try different numbers in
lines 40 to 60 but they must not
exceed the max values in your
list. You may need to experiment
and I am assuming the fonts you
have are 16 dots wide (line 50)
so you may need to adjust that.
They could be 8 or 24 dots wide
for all I know! Send me one of
your fonts if you have trouble
here so I can examine it.

Make sure you include all the
semi-colons (;) in the above as
I think you may get a linefeed
when you don't want one!

Following the above,your printer
should be awaiting the actual
font data ("data" in your list)
and this is done thus...

You must first load the font in
your computer's memory. Any free
area will do but let's use say,
32768. To load it and send it to
your printer you need to know
the length of the font code. On
SAM, Disciple and +D you can get
this using DIR 1. The length is
the number on the far right of
the filename. Other users will
need a header reader if they do
not know the length. Suppose the
length is'L'.Add to the program:

70 LOAD "FONTNAME" CODE 32768

80 LPRINT MEM$(32768 TO 32767+L)
                         (SAM)
or...
   FOR N=32768 TO 32767+L:
   LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N; : NEXT N
                      (Spectrum)

Obviously, you can add 32767 to
the length and put the sum where
I have put 32767+L.

A 24-bit font is needed so I
just don't know if the fonts you
have are suitable. Let me know.

Next you must add the number of
characters which is 96. This is
the bit at the end which says:
n2-n1+1 and you get it from 127
(the final character in the font
- the copyright sign) MINUS 32
(the SPACE character) PLUS 1. If
you only send a few characters
you must change that along with
the numbers in lines 20 and 30.

Finally, SAVE the program so you
can use it again or change it if
there's an error!

Having SAVEd it you can now RUN
the program and the font should
download. When you want to use
the new font you must use...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 1;

Thereafter anything you print
should use the new font so you
could add a test line to the
program...

110 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 1;

120 CLOSE #3: OPEN #3;"T"
      (+3 use FORMAT LPRINT "E",
       +D use POKE @6,0)

130 LPRINT "MESSAGE..."

Line 120 is to end sending codes
ready to send ordinary text.

To switch back to the printer's
own font you need to use...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 0;

           ...but remember, you
MUST always use OPEN #3;"B"
before sending codes (unless you
have previously opened it).

If you have problems please let
me know and preferably send me a
copy of your font on disc and
any print-out you may have done.

I regret I don't have a 24-pin
printer so can't test this so if
anyone else spots a fault or,
indeed can give us info on how
to download 24-bit fonts, please
let us all know!
                        - Brian

From: William Coats,STRATHCLYDE

Dear Brian/Ron,

As this is my first letter to
you let me start off by thanking
you for such a great "magazine"
and, after your recent price
restructuring, a great bargain!

Re: your answer to D. Green of
Sheffield about Fontwist.2 (OUT-
LET 51) you asked for feedback
on loading and downloading of
fonts on printers.

My set up is a +3 (the one that
needs POKEs to 23354/23355) and
a Citizen 120D+ printer. I
managed to get your program to
load the fonts into the printer
- with one or two alterations...

Line 1105 (the attr byte) has to
go before line 1100.

Line 6200 to read...

6200 GO SUB 9886: FOR a=33536 TO
33536+(L-1) : PRINT AT 10,13;A:
LPRINT CHR$ PEEK A;: NEXT A
(the PRINT in the line lets you
see the bytes downloading.

Line 9895 becomes 9896.

Insert new line...

9895 LPRINT CHR$(27);":";CHR$(0)
;CHR$(0);CHR$(0)
(this copies the current font in
ROM to RAM and so can be altered
- if you want to alter just a
few characters.

On the 120D+ you have to rotate
anti-clockwise and mirror. Each
character is made up on a matrix
6 columns wide by 9 rows deep,
so you have 6 dots in a row plus
5 dots in the lines between the
columns. The limitation on the
120D+ is that you cannot define
a character which has two
immediately-adjacent dots, i.e.
one in a box and one on the line
next to it, in the same row.

Now for my problem! If I reset
the computer, load in a program
for printing, the printer
doesn't operate. But if I BREAK
back to BASIC then RUN the
program again it works fine. Is
this a fault in the computer or
in the printer?

Finally, has there ever been a
text compressor/decompressor for
"OUTLET" files in any of the
back issues?

                    Bill Coats

Brian Cavers to Bill Coats.

Thanks, Bill.

Re: the changes to FONTWIST, I
think you have restricted it to
the +3 only! To make it easier
for everyone else I have made
your mods myself except for the
+3 restriction and put it in
this month's ADD-ENDERS as the
new... FONTWIST.3! Let me know
if I've messed it up, Bill!

No, we've never put our text
compressor in OUTLET as it's
rather specialized but if you
are into machine code then the
next letter from Francis Miles
has a routine you may like to
experiment with!

Regarding the oddity where the
printer doesn't operate until
you BREAK and re-RUN the program
this seems to be a +3 bug. Which
program or programs are you
referring to? You say you are
already using the POKEs to 23354
and 23355 and that doesn't help?
Does FORMAT LPRINT "U" or "E"
help? Have you any programs that
DO print correctly without this
problem?

                        - Brian.

From: Francis G. Miles, WELWYN


Dear Ron and Brian

I think I invented the SYS.PT
routine given by S D Trotter in
OUTLETTERS, Issue no.53. Well,
actually I know I did: I
described it in a series I did a
year or two ago in FORMAT called
"Machine code made easy". But,
of course, somebody else may
have invented it too.

I have an extension of this
routine which saves a lot of
repetitive messages. (Messages
use up memory faster than
anything else)like in adventures
for example.

Put somewhere in your m/c a list
of "coded words": each word must
have its last character flagged
with the high bit set.

E.g.,

   codwd defb 128
   ;0 MOVE space
         defm 'MOVE'
         defb ' '+128'
   ;1 BACK no space
         defm 'BAC'
         defb 'K'+128
   ;2 AT 7,11
         defb 22,7,11+128
   ;3 etc

Note the list starts with a 128
byte.  You can have a maximum of
127 coded words numbered 0-126.

Now the SYSPT2 routine is like
this:

  syspt2 ex (sp),hl
          1d a,(hl)
          inc hl
          ex (sp),hl
          cp 255
          ret z
  ;if hi zero,
          bit 7,a
          jr nz,sp1
  ;print byte and loop
          rst 10h
          jr syspt2
  ;hi set: use code word
   spl     1d,codwd
  ;strip hi bit for counter
          and 01111111b
  ;ROM finds start of a 'th word
          call 3137;po.search

  ;loop to print word
  sp2     1d a,(de)
  ;strip hi bit before printing
          and 01111111b
          rst 10h
  ;double a for hi bit check:
          ld a,(de)
          inc de
  ;if hi bit off loop for next
          add a
          jr nc,sp2
  ;else loop to start
          jr syspt2
          defb 2+128;AT 7,11
          defb 0+128;MOVE space
          defb 1+128;BACK
          defm 'ONCE'
          defb 25;end
My normal royalty fee is a
bottle of Scotch for each use of
my routines, but this is purely
voluntary in this case.F.G.MILES

From: Mark Payne,
      5 Bassett Road, Coundon,
  COVENTRY, W. Midlands CV6 1LF

Dear Ron & Brian,

As you seem to know almost
everything about the Sinclair
computers I thought I would ask
you for some help.

I have a large collection of
records and I have been using
TASWORD 2 to keep a list of them
but one thing TASWORD cannot do
is to sort the entries into
alphabetical order. This would
be of enormous use as when I
needed to find a record I would
not have to sort through my
entire list to find a particular
item.

If you would include my address
so other people can reply to my
letter, I'd be most grateful.

Also as a new member to OUTLET I
have noticed that it is 80% for
the serious user. Would you be
willing to include a large,good-
quality game in your issues (say
once every 3 months).

           Mark Payne


Brian Cavers to Mark Payne

Yes, I'm willing! You send 'em,
I'll put 'em in! Seriously, we
can only publish what is sent to
us. I have less and less time to
write large programs myself so I
cannot apply myself to this. As
it stands anyway, we often have
games: BREAKTHRU' (Issue 21),
CARNIVAL CAPERS (16),COLOUR BIND
(25), GLOBULAR TROUBLE (29),
GOLDEN COBRA (18), KEMSHU (23),
SHANGHAI (24), SPIN IT (26),
TRAILRACER (47), TRAKTRAP (15),
ULTIMATE WARRIOR (41), WITCHWOOD
3D (19), SANTA (52) and loads
and loads more!If you mean games
that could sell for `9.99 and
earn thousands of pounds then we
await such with bated breath!

Regarding sorting your Tasword 2
files this might not be too
difficult if each item to be
sorted uses the same number of
lines. Please send one of your
files for me to look at as a lot
depends on how it is set out. Do
you put one item on each line?
Is the name to be sorted at the
start of the line or in the
middle? Are there gaps between
lines?

Instead of Tasword 2, what you
should have used is a database(a
record-keeping program) which
would sort them how you like.
Still, it may be possible to
sort them as they are.
                      - Brian

From: Brian Jones, WARRINGTON

Dear Ron and Brian,

I was impressed with my first
copies of OUTLET No 52 and 35,
However,I seem to have a problem
with 'Hiform' on Issue 35.

When a disc is formatted to 203k
using Multiface to transfer from
173 to 203k I need at least 10k
spare i.e., if a program is 43k
my +3 will not write a full
program to a 203k disc unless
there is at least 53k left - any
less and it comes up with
"I.O. Error".

I hope you could shed some light
on this problem as it does not
happen on a 173k disc.   - BRIAN

Brian Cavers to Brian Jones

Yes, clearly the Multiface does
not check the disc correctly but
assumes a normal format. There's
nothing that can be done about
this. The limitation is with the
Multiface which can't be changed
so all you can do is make sure
you have enough room. Is it
possible to copy Multiface files
to another disc using the +3
COPY or MOVE commands? If so, at
least you can pack them on a
disc afterwards, if you want to
use space as economically as
possible.If they don't copy then
you can only add normal files to
a disc later to fill it up.

                        - Brian

Dear Ron and Brian,

I should like to know if Enrico
Maria Giordano's PD comms
program 'LINK' that I sent you
three months ago will be
published in OUTLET.

I'd also like an 'ADD-ENDERS'
collection for Opus Discovery
users like me. Please note that
many of us now own a second
drive 3.5" DS/DD 720K in
position 1 or 2 and it's a pity
that we can't share all that
useful information and programs.

Finally, could you inform us
about how many Spectrum and Sam
users are subscribing to each
version of OUTLET? It would be
very interesting to know it.

I hope you will publish my
address, especially for those
users interested in communicaton
and data exchange between
Spectrum and other computers.

          Kind regards,

              Carlo


Brian Cavers > Carlo Maluntrucco

Yes, I'm sorry about the delay
but we do have a backlog queue
of contributions and some need
more preparation and so get held
back a while. If I remember, the
LINK program has a large number
of different files and it is not
(or may not be!) straightforward
in its integration into OUTLET!

Pity about ADD-ENDERS. My guess
is it may often fill an Opus
disc on its own or even be too
big! Even if I had time and did
this for Opus, you might still
have to pay the price of OUTLET
for each disc to cover our costs
and labour. I can only suggest
you get back-issue tape versions
instead.

I'm not happy about this. I'd
much prefer to provide all the
various things that people ask
for but the hard truth is that
already many of the services we
do are not economic and are
foolish from a commercial point
of view. I wish I could wave a
magic wand!

The only other thing I can
suggest is that if any Opus user
(or group of users) would like
to organise this themselves and
order tape back issues and put
ADD-ENDERS on Opus disc then I
will give them permission to
copy such discs free of charge
to any other OUTLET reader. Thus
you may share the costs. I trust
you not to take advantage!

To be fair, the same goes for
microdrive users but in either
case I'd like the minimum hassle
for myself! I suggest anyone
willing to organise it write in
and I will publish their name
and full address then others can
write direct to them until you
feel you have enough. You don't,
after all, have to order every
issue if there are only a very
few of you.

This can be a continuing thing
and not limited to back issues
but each new issue if you want.

If you try this I suggest you
just dump the lot on the disc
rather than try linking it to a
CONTENTS page!

Well,we had no really up-to-date
figures for OUTLET sales and
funnily enough, our new database
cannot actually print unit sales
so we had to rush round trying
to extract some meaningful sums
from our system (as up to about
last December).We find both Opus
and microdrive subscriptions are
now well below 100 each but
steady, Disciple around 250,tape
around 100, +3 around 250 and
SAM about 300 so overall it is
over the 1000 mark.We can always
use more so anyone reading this,
why not make sure everyone YOU
know gets to hear about OUTLET!
It's to your advantage: the more
readers, the more contributions,
the higher the quality and the
more we can keep down the price!

SELECT USER ESC %  DEFINED CHARACTER SET

Dec.        27 37 n

Discussion  The value of n is a binary number that identifies either a resident character set or a down-loaded one.

01H (1 decimal) Specifies a downloaded set

The printer ignores this command if the font is not loaded.

ESC &   SPECIFY USER DEFINED CHARACTERS

Function:Specifies user designed character sets

Sequence:ESC & 00 n1 n2 [d1 d2 d3 data...] n2-n1+1

Hex      1B 26 00 n1 n2 [d1 d2 d3 data...] n2-n1+1

DEC      27 38 0  n1 n2 [d1 d2 d3 data...] n2-n1+1

Discussion: All parameters are binary numbers. n1 and n2 identify the start and end codes to be defined.

d1 sets the amount of space you want to add to the left of the character, d2 the pattern width and d3 sets the space to the right. The parameters d1 d2 d3 must satisfy these conditions:-

```text
            d2          d1+d2+d3
```

Mode  (max.value)  (max.value)

```text
  ----  -----------  -----------
```

Draft mode    9          12 LQ mode at

```text
10 cpi       29          36
```

LQ mode at

```text
12 cpi       23          30
```

LQ mode at

```text
15 cpi       15          24
```

Proportional pitch        38          42

The data defines the character pattern. In normal mode, each character requires three bytes of data (d2*3).

A dot column represents three data bytes in normal mode and two data bytes in superscript/ subscript mode. The msb of the first byte corresponds to the top pin of the column,while the lsb of the third byte (in normal mode) corresponds to the bottom pin. Each character with a code between n1 and n2 must be defined. This means that...

d2*3*(n2-n1+1) or d2*3*(n2-n1+1) data bytes are required.

Brian Cavers to Ken Stearn

In BASIC, you use the LPRINT command to send data to your printer and each piece of data is a number between 0 and 255. However, the SAM Coupe and most Spectrum printer interfaces have two"modes" of sending this data: as pure code or in "expanded" form. In this expanded form many of the codes are stopped by the computer and instead, a keyword is sent. This is for printing a BASIC listing etc. To switch the printer to do things like BOLD printing or ITALICS you need to send "control" codes. To do this you need first to make sure your computer is in the "pure code" mode as follows...

To send control codes, first:

OPEN #3;"B"          SAM COUPE, OPUS,MDRIVE

POKE @6,1            DISCIPLE/+D

FORMAT LPRINT "U"    +3

COPY: REM CHR$ 0     KEMPSTON E

After, use LPRINT to send codes. For example, to send code 65 you LPRINT CHR$ 65. Codes between 32 and 127 also have an "ASCII" equivalent so you can use that instead if you know it. To find it just enter,e.g.,PRINT CHR$ 65 and you will see a capital A on your computer screen so you can use LPRINT "A" instead of the LPRINT CHR$ 65 if you want!

I mention that because you may wonder what the printer manual means when it's got ESC &. This means the code for ESC (which is 27) and "&" (code 38) so that could be sent to the printer with either...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;CHR$ 38;  or...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;"&";

...it means the same. If you enter PRINT CHR$ 38 you will see a "&" on your screen.If you enter PRINT CODE "&" you will see 38 printed on your screen.Get it? Under the heading ESC & in your list next to DEC you will see it starts 27 38 0 plus other things so enter...

10 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"&";CHR$ 0; (tells printer,font is coming)

20 LPRINT CHR$ 32; (first character. - the SPACE character. This is n1 in your list)

30 LPRINT CHR$ 127; (last character, the copyright sign. This is n2 in your list)

40 LPRINT CHR$ 0; (left gap width before character. This is d1)

50 LPRINT CHR$ 16; (character pattern width. d2)

60 LPRINT CHR$ 4; (right gap width. d3)

You can try different numbers in lines 40 to 60 but they must not exceed the max values in your list. You may need to experiment and I am assuming the fonts you have are 16 dots wide (line 50) so you may need to adjust that. They could be 8 or 24 dots wide for all I know! Send me one of your fonts if you have trouble here so I can examine it.

Make sure you include all the semi-colons (;) in the above as I think you may get a linefeed when you don't want one!

Following the above,your printer should be awaiting the actual font data ("data" in your list) and this is done thus...

You must first load the font in your computer's memory. Any free area will do but let's use say, 32768. To load it and send it to your printer you need to know the length of the font code. On SAM, Disciple and +D you can get this using DIR 1. The length is the number on the far right of the filename. Other users will need a header reader if they do not know the length. Suppose the length is'L'.Add to the program:

70 LOAD "FONTNAME" CODE 32768

80 LPRINT MEM$(32768 TO 32767+L)

```text
                         (SAM)
```

or... FOR N=32768 TO 32767+L: LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N; : NEXT N (Spectrum)

Obviously, you can add 32767 to the length and put the sum where I have put 32767+L.

A 24-bit font is needed so I just don't know if the fonts you have are suitable. Let me know.

Next you must add the number of characters which is 96. This is the bit at the end which says: n2-n1+1 and you get it from 127 (the final character in the font - the copyright sign) MINUS 32 (the SPACE character) PLUS 1. If you only send a few characters you must change that along with the numbers in lines 20 and 30.

Finally, SAVE the program so you can use it again or change it if there's an error!

Having SAVEd it you can now RUN the program and the font should download. When you want to use the new font you must use...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 1;

Thereafter anything you print should use the new font so you could add a test line to the program...

110 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 1;

120 CLOSE #3: OPEN #3;"T" (+3 use FORMAT LPRINT "E", +D use POKE @6,0)

130 LPRINT "MESSAGE..."

Line 120 is to end sending codes ready to send ordinary text.

To switch back to the printer's own font you need to use...

LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 0;

...but remember, you MUST always use OPEN #3;"B" before sending codes (unless you have previously opened it).

If you have problems please let me know and preferably send me a copy of your font on disc and any print-out you may have done.

I regret I don't have a 24-pin printer so can't test this so if anyone else spots a fault or, indeed can give us info on how to download 24-bit fonts, please let us all know!

```text
                        - Brian
```

### Brian Cavers — Ken Stearn

В BASIC для отправки данных на принтер используется команда `LPRINT`, и каждый элемент данных представляет собой число от 0 до 255. Однако у SAM Coupe и большинства принтерных интерфейсов для Spectrum есть два «режима» отправки этих данных: в виде чистого кода или в «расширенном» (expanded) виде. В этом расширенном режиме многие коды перехватываются компьютером, и вместо них отправляется ключевое слово (токен). Это сделано для печати листингов BASIC и т. п. Чтобы переключить принтер на такие вещи, как жирный шрифт (BOLD) или курсив (ITALICS), вам нужно отправлять «управляющие» коды. Для этого сначала необходимо убедиться, что компьютер переведён в режим «чистого кода», следующим образом...

Чтобы отправлять управляющие коды, сначала выполните:

```text
OPEN #3;"B"          SAM COUPE, OPUS, MDRIVE
POKE @6,1            DISCIPLE/+D
FORMAT LPRINT "U"    +3
COPY: REM CHR$ 0     KEMPSTON E
```

После этого используйте `LPRINT` для отправки кодов. Например, чтобы отправить код 65, вы пишете `LPRINT CHR$ 65`. Коды от 32 до 127 также имеют эквивалент в «ASCII», поэтому, если вы его знаете, можно использовать сам символ. Чтобы узнать его, просто введите, например, `PRINT CHR$ 65`, и на экране появится заглавная буква A, так что при желании вместо `LPRINT CHR$ 65` можно написать `LPRINT "A"`!

Я упоминаю это потому, что вам может быть непонятно, что имеет в виду руководство к принтеру, когда там написано «ESC &». Это означает код клавиши ESC (то есть 27) и «&» (код 38), так что на принтер это можно отправить либо так...

```text
LPRINT CHR$ 27;CHR$ 38;
```

...либо так:

```text
LPRINT CHR$ 27;"&";
```

...это абсолютно одно и то же. Если вы введёте `PRINT CHR$ 38`, на экране появится «&». Если вы введёте `PRINT CODE "&"`, на экране напечатается 38. Понятно? Под заголовком ESC & в вашем списке рядом с DEC вы увидите, что последовательность начинается с 27 38 0 плюс другие параметры, поэтому введите...

```text
10 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"&";CHR$ 0;
  (сообщает принтеру, что далее идёт шрифт)

20 LPRINT CHR$ 32;
   (первый символ — символ ПРОБЕЛА.
   В вашем списке это n1)

30 LPRINT CHR$ 127;
  (последний символ, знак копирайта.
  В вашем списке это n2)

40 LPRINT CHR$ 0;
          (ширина отступа слева перед
          символом. Это d1)

50 LPRINT CHR$ 16;
   (ширина матрицы символа. d2)

60 LPRINT CHR$ 4;
           (ширина отступа справа. d3)
```

Вы можете попробовать разные числа в строках 40–60, но они не должны превышать максимальные значения из вашего списка. Возможно, придётся поэкспериментировать; я предполагаю, что ваши шрифты имеют ширину 16 точек (строка 50), так что это значение, возможно, потребуется скорректировать. Насколько мне известно, они могут быть шириной и 8, и 24 точки! Если возникнут трудности, пришлите мне один из ваших шрифтов, чтобы я мог его изучить.

Обязательно ставьте все точки с запятой (;) в приведённых выше строках, иначе, боюсь, вы получите перевод строки там, где он совсем не нужен!

После этого ваш принтер должен ожидать фактические данные шрифта («data» в вашем списке), и делается это так...

Сначала необходимо загрузить шрифт в память компьютера. Подойдёт любая свободная область, но давайте возьмём, скажем, 32768. Чтобы загрузить его и отправить на принтер, нужно знать длину кода шрифта. На SAM, Disciple и +D её можно узнать с помощью команды `DIR 1`. Длина — это число в крайнем правом столбце напротив имени файла. Другим пользователям, если они не знают точную длину, понадобится программа для чтения заголовков (header reader). Предположим, длина равна 'L'. Добавьте в программу:

```text
70 LOAD "FONTNAME" CODE 32768

80 LPRINT MEM$(32768 TO 32767+L)
                         (SAM)
или...
   FOR N=32768 TO 32767+L:
   LPRINT CHR$ PEEK N; : NEXT N
                      (Spectrum)
```

Разумеется, вы можете просто прибавить 32767 к длине и вписать полученную сумму вместо выражения `32767+L`.

Требуется 24-битный шрифт, поэтому я просто не знаю, подходят ли те шрифты, которые у вас есть. Дайте мне знать.

Затем нужно добавить количество символов, равное 96. Это та часть формулы в конце, где сказано: `n2-n1+1`; получается оно вычитанием 32 (символ ПРОБЕЛА) из 127 (последний символ в шрифте — знак копирайта) ПЛЮС 1. Если вы отправляете только несколько символов, эту величину нужно изменить вместе с числами в строках 20 и 30.

Наконец, сохраните программу (`SAVE`), чтобы её можно было использовать снова или исправить в случае ошибки!

Сохранив её, вы можете запустить программу (`RUN`), и шрифт должен загрузиться в принтер. Когда вы захотите использовать новый шрифт, отправьте команду...

После этого всё, что вы печатаете, должно выводиться новым шрифтом, так что можно добавить в программу тестовую строку...


Строка 120 завершает передачу кодов и подготавливает принтер к приёму обычного текста.

Чтобы переключиться обратно на собственный шрифт принтера, используйте...

```text
LPRINT CHR$ 27;"%";CHR$ 0;
```

...но помните: вы ВСЕГДА должны давать команду `OPEN #3;"B"` перед отправкой управляющих кодов (если только этот поток не был открыт ранее).

Поместите где-нибудь в памяти список «закодированных слов»: у каждого слова последний символ должен быть помечен установленным старшим битом.

Например:

```text
   codwd defb 128
   ;0 MOVE с пробелом
         defm 'MOVE'
         defb ' '+128
   ;1 BACK без пробела
         defm 'BAC'
         defb 'K'+128
   ;2 AT 7,11
         defb 22,7,11+128
   ;3 и т.д.
```

Обратите внимание: список начинается с байта 128. Всего может быть максимум 127 закодированных слов с номерами от 0 до 126.

Сама процедура SYSPT2 выглядит так:

```text
  syspt2 ex (sp),hl
         ld a,(hl)
         inc hl
         ex (sp),hl
         cp 255
         ret z
  ;если бит 7 сброшен,
         bit 7,a
         jr nz,sp1
  ;печатаем байт и зацикливаемся
         rst 10h
         jr syspt2
  ;бит 7 установлен: используем кодовое слово
   sp1   ld de,codwd
  ;сбрасываем старший бит для счетчика
         and 01111111b
  ;ПЗУ ищет начало n-го слова
         call 3137;po.search

  ;цикл печати слова
  sp2    ld a,(de)
  ;сбрасываем старший бит перед печатью
         and 01111111b
         rst 10h
  ;удваиваем a для проверки старшего бита:
         ld a,(de)
         inc de
  ;если старший бит был 0, берем следующий символ
         add a
         jr nc,sp2
  ;иначе переходим в начало
         jr syspt2
         defb 2+128;AT 7,11
         defb 0+128;MOVE с пробелом
         defb 1+128;BACK
         defm 'ONCE'
         defb 255;конец
```

Мой обычный авторский гонорар — бутылка скотча за каждое использование моих процедур, но в данном случае это дело чисто добровольное. F.G.MILES
